reference.source: Respiratory Medicine and Dermatology reference texts
clinicalPearls: Classic triad of yellow, thickened, slow-growing dystrophic nails, lymphoedema, and respiratory manifestations, though not all three need be present
Pleural effusions are the hallmark respiratory feature and are typically exudative, sometimes chylous, and often recurrent
Other respiratory features include chronic cough, bronchiectasis, and recurrent sinopulmonary infections
Nails show a yellow-green discolouration, transverse over-curvature, absent lunula and cuticle, and may lift from the nail bed (onycholysis)
Usually seen in middle-aged or older adults and generally sporadic rather than inherited
An association with malignancy and immunodeficiency is recognised, so a search for occult disease may be warranted
Diagnosis is clinical, based on recognising the characteristic combination of features, as no specific test exists
reference.pathophysiology: Yellow nail syndrome is thought to reflect a functional or structural abnormality of lymphatic drainage, with impaired and often ectatic lymphatics leading to the peripheral lymphoedema, pleural effusions, and impaired clearance predisposing to bronchiectasis and sinus disease. The abnormal lymphatic function is believed to slow nail growth and cause the characteristic discolouration and thickening. Microvascular and lymphatic dysfunction, sometimes with associated protein leakage, underlies the exudative and occasionally chylous nature of the effusions. The precise cause is unknown, and the syndrome is generally acquired, sometimes appearing in association with malignancy, autoimmune disease, or immunodeficiency.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital or acquired lymphoedema of other cause
Nephrotic syndrome or hypoalbuminaemia causing effusions and oedema
Chylothorax from thoracic duct injury or malignancy
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment of the characteristic nail changes, lymphoedema, and effusions
Pleural fluid analysis to characterise the effusion as exudative or chylous
Chest imaging including CT to assess effusions and bronchiectasis
Nail examination and, where needed, exclusion of fungal infection
Investigation for associated malignancy or immunodeficiency when clinically indicated
Lymphoscintigraphy in selected cases to assess lymphatic function
redFlags: Features suggesting underlying malignancy requiring investigation
Large or rapidly reaccumulating pleural effusions causing breathlessness
Recurrent severe respiratory infections indicating significant bronchiectasis or immunodeficiency
Chylous effusion prompting evaluation of the thoracic duct and lymphatics
reference.prognosis: The course is chronic and variable; nail changes may occasionally improve spontaneously, respiratory and lymphatic features often persist and require symptomatic management, and prognosis is influenced by any associated malignancy or immunodeficiency.
pitfalls: Dismissing the nail changes as simple fungal infection and missing the syndrome
Failing to recognise the association with occult malignancy
Attributing recurrent effusions to more common causes without considering the triad
Overlooking bronchiectasis as a driver of recurrent infection
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
